title: DSA Practice in Six Languages
description: Try small questions about lists, searching, sorting, trees, and graphs. Read code in your language, predict its result, and fix a mistake. You can repeat each task.

exercises.question: Which part is the algorithm in the score example?
options: The steps that add each score to a total
The name of the programming language
exercises.explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps. The array holds the scores; the adding steps work on those scores.

exercises.question: Which DSA language examples can run directly in this site's browser playground?
exercises.explanation: The site can run JavaScript in the browser. C, C++, Python, C#, and Java need their separate local language tools.

exercises.question: A search checks every item when a target is missing. How many checks does it need for 5 items?
exercises.explanation: There are 5 items and each is checked once. A missing target makes the search reach the end.

exercises.question: Which indexes are valid for an array with 4 items?
exercises.explanation: The first index is 0. Four items end at index 3, which is length minus 1.

exercises.question: What tells this linked-list walk to stop?
options: The current link has no node
exercises.explanation: The last node points to no next node. After following that empty link, the loop condition is false.

exercises.question: You push 2, then 5, then 8. Which item does the next pop return?
exercises.explanation: A stack removes the last item pushed. The newest item is 8, so it is at the top.

exercises.question: A queue receives 2, then 5, then 8. Which item leaves first?
exercises.explanation: A queue serves the first item that joined. Item 2 has waited the longest.

exercises.question: How many distinct values are in a set made from 2, 2, 5, 5, and 8?
exercises.explanation: The distinct values are 2, 5, and 8. Repeated copies do not add new set items.

exercises.question: A map has key 2 with value 3. You set key 2 to value 6. What happens?
exercises.explanation: A map keeps one value for each key. Setting an existing key replaces its value.

exercises.question: Keys 5 and 9 both start at slot 1. What is this called?
exercises.explanation: A collision happens when different keys choose the same starting slot. The table must keep both keys safely.

exercises.question: Which position does this search return for 4 in [9, 4, 7, 4]?
exercises.explanation: It scans from the left and stops at the first 4. That item is at position 1 because positions start at 0.

exercises.question: Which list is ready for the binary search shown here?
exercises.explanation: The search expects values from small to large. Only [2, 4, 6, 8] has that order.

exercises.question: What is the ascending numeric order of [10, 2, 30]?
exercises.explanation: Ascending numeric order means smallest to largest. The value 2 is smaller than 10, and 30 is the largest.

exercises.question: After the first full bubble sort pass on [4, 2, 3, 1], where is 4?
exercises.explanation: Each neighbour comparison moves 4 one step right. At the end of the first pass, 4 is at the last position.

exercises.question: What does selection sort choose on each pass?
options: The largest item in the finished part
The smallest item in the unfinished part
exercises.explanation: The smallest unfinished item belongs in the next position on the left. The algorithm finds it, then swaps it into that position.

exercises.question: While inserting 2 into the sorted part [1, 3, 4], which values shift right?
exercises.explanation: Values larger than 2 must move right to make a gap. The 1 stays put, and 2 goes after it.

exercises.question: What is the base case in the shown sum function?
options: Always call with the same n
exercises.explanation: At n = 0, there are no positive numbers left to add. Returning 0 gives an immediate answer and stops further calls.

exercises.question: When merging [2, 4] and [1, 3], which number is taken first?
exercises.explanation: Both parts are already sorted. Their smallest remaining values are at the front, so compare 2 with 1 and take 1.

exercises.question: In this quick sort, which item is chosen as the pivot?
options: The last value in the current part
Always the first value in the whole list
exercises.explanation: The code reads a[high]. high is the last position of the current part, so its value becomes the pivot.

exercises.question: In a sorted list, the end values sum to less than the target. Which marker moves?
exercises.explanation: The current left value is too small even with the largest remaining partner. Moving left rightward chooses a larger or equal value.

exercises.question: Which node is a leaf?
exercises.explanation: A leaf ends a branch because it has no children. The root can also be a leaf in a one-node tree.

exercises.question: At a BST node holding 8, which branch can contain target 3?
exercises.explanation: Under the strict BST rule, all smaller values are in the left branch. Three is smaller than eight.

exercises.question: Which value is always at the root of a non-empty min-heap?
exercises.explanation: Every parent is no larger than its children. Following that rule down from the root makes the root a minimum.

exercises.question: Which visit order does inorder traversal follow?
exercises.explanation: Inorder first finishes the left branch, then records the current node, and finally visits the right branch.

exercises.question: There are edges 0-1 and 0-2 only. Who are the direct neighbours of vertex 0?
exercises.explanation: Each direct edge from 0 names one neighbour. Its edges connect to 1 and to 2.

exercises.question: When should this BFS mark a newly found node seen?
options: Only after every node has been visited
exercises.explanation: Marking at the moment of adding prevents a second neighbour from adding the same waiting node again.

exercises.question: Why does DFS mark a node before visiting its neighbours?
options: To stop a cycle from calling back into it as if it were new
To make all paths equally short
exercises.explanation: A neighbour can have a link back to the current node. Marking first lets that link be skipped instead of starting a repeated visit.

exercises.question: If ways[3] is 3 and ways[4] is 5, how many one-or-two-step plans reach stair 5?
exercises.explanation: The final move comes from stair 4 or stair 3. Add their saved counts: 5 + 3 = 8.

exercises.question: What does this stack print? Read the last line carefully.
exercises.explanation: push adds 9 at the top. pop removes that newest item, so the result is 9.

exercises.question: Which value does this C program print?
exercises.explanation: Array positions start at 0. Position 1 is the second value, which is 8.

exercises.question: What is at the front after the first item leaves?
exercises.explanation: A queue serves the oldest item first. Removing 3 leaves 7 at the front.

exercises.question: How many different values does this set hold?
exercises.explanation: A set keeps each value once. The values are 2, 5, and 8, so its size is 3.

exercises.question: What score does this C# program print?
exercises.explanation: Writing a new value for the same key replaces the old value. Asha now has 9.

exercises.question: How many visits does this Java loop count?
exercises.explanation: The loop visits four items. It counts visits; it does not add the values.

exercises.question: We want number order: 2, 6, 10. Which change fixes the result?
exercises.explanation: Without a number comparison, JavaScript sort compares text. The comparison a - b puts smaller numbers first.

exercises.question: This C loop reads past the array. Which loop condition is safe?
exercises.explanation: Three items have indexes 0, 1, and 2. The condition i < 3 stops before the invalid index 3.

exercises.question: The stack has no items. What should we check before reading its top?
exercises.explanation: There is no top item in an empty stack. First check that the stack is not empty. Reading or removing a missing item is unsafe.

exercises.question: The loop below uses binary search. What is wrong with its input?
options: The values must be sorted first
A list must have an odd length
exercises.explanation: Binary search safely removes half only when the list is sorted. It may work by luck on an unsorted list, but can miss other values.

exercises.question: Ben is missing from the map. Which action avoids reading a missing key?
options: Print the number of letters in Ben
exercises.explanation: TryGetValue checks whether a key exists. If it returns false, show a missing-value message instead of reading with the indexer.

exercises.question: Which index reads the last item without an error?
exercises.explanation: The length is 3 but the last index is 2. For a nonempty array, the last index is length minus 1.

exercises.question: Finish findIndex so it returns the first matching index, or -1 when no value matches.
checklist: Check every item from index zero.
Return an index, not the matching value.
Return -1 only after all items have been checked.
Try an empty list, a missing value, and repeated values.
exercises.explanation: Visit items from left to right. Return as soon as one matches. The return after the loop handles missing values and an empty list.

exercises.question: Use left and right pointers to reverse a copy of the list. Keep the original list unchanged.
checklist: Copy the input before changing any items.
Swap left and right, then move both inward.
Stop when the pointers meet or cross.
Check an empty list and a list with one item.
exercises.explanation: Each swap puts two items into place. Stop when left is not smaller than right. The copy takes O(n) extra space; the loop takes O(n) time.
